articles.title: CNN analysis uncovers construction flaws in public housing towers that collapsed during Venezuela quakes
articles.summary: A CNN analysis of videos and images of some of the buildings suggests that flaws in their construction may have contributed to the mass tragedy.
articles.body: The day after massive dual earthquakes shattered Venezuela, Ailin Quiroz made her way toward the coast to search for her sister. She found only a mountain of rubble where her apartment building had once stood. Quiroz climbed through the ruins for hours but found no trace of her sister or six other relatives who lived in the 13-story tower. Now, she’s tormented by a question: Why did their building collapse while other nearby high-rises survived? The building was one of 15 public housing towers in the coastal town of Caraballeda that collapsed in the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes on June 24. Though the government has yet to release a comprehensive list of people killed, thousands of public housing residents likely perished in the disaster. Each tower, over eight stories tall, had at least 240 apartments. A CNN analysis of videos and images of some of those buildings — both during an extraordinarily fast construction process and after their collapse — suggests that construction flaws may have contributed to the mass tragedy. That visual evidence appears to show improperly assembled rebar supports — steel bars meant to reinforce the strength of concrete — in apparent building code violations at five government-built complexes, where the 15 collapsed towers once stood. In three of the complexes, images also show deep-seated rust in metal supports, which experts say could be a sign of poor-quality concrete. It is unclear whether these building defects were present in every government-built tower that fell. Experts in structural engineering, Venezuelan building practices, and seismology who reviewed evidence of the defects said those faults could have made the towers more prone to collapsing in massive earthquakes, though they also cautioned that it’s difficult to prove a direct cause following the massive tremors. “This is how a concrete structure fails if it’s not done right,” structural engineer Kit Miyamoto explained while on the ground in Caracas. Immediately after the earthquakes, a government commission was established to analyze affected buildings. Nearly 100 buildings are being analyzed using material samples and measurements, commission President Francisco Garcés told CNN. One disaster to the next For nearly a decade, residents had complained of problems in the towers, which were commissioned in 2011 by then-Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez. Local media reported dozens of residents’ complaints about persistent water intrusion, damaged pipes, and sewage leaks. The 15 towers that later fell were among dozens built across Venezuela by the Chávez regime, many intended to house families displaced by a flooding and landslide disaster in 2010. Located near the San Sebastián fault line on Venezuela’s coast, their construction came under the responsibility of the Presidential Office of Special Plans and Projects (OPPPE), which Chávez had created two years earlier as part of his sweeping ambition to build three million homes in nine years. These housing developments were constructed in barely a year. The Office of Special Plans and Projects’ then director and chief architect — Chávez’s longtime friend Francisco Sesto — detailed the process in his personal blog, writing that the president demanded 200,000 homes to be built in 2012 alone, the year of their construction. Former OPPPE principal Lucas Pou told CNN it was standard practice for the Office to award no-bid contracts under an emergency directive to help speed things along but said he hadn’t worked on the Caraballeda housing projects. In his blog, Sesto describes the OPPPE’s mission as “a gigantic effort carried out with an intensity never before seen in Venezuela.” To stay on schedule, he wrote, construction teams rotated through two to three shifts every day. Sesto did not respond to CNN’s multiple requests for comment on this story but told The New York Times that he does not consider it “journalistically sound to focus on a handful of Great Mission buildings that collapsed, given that hundreds of private buildings also collapsed.” While tens of thousands of buildings collapsed from the quakes, these OPPPE developments were among the largest residential buildings to fall in coastal La Guaira state. Satellite imagery shows that in Caraballeda, 63% of all high-rise towers built by a special public housing authority collapsed. Interim President Delcy Rodríguez ordered the suspension of the OPPPE in February, a few months before the earthquakes. Rebar issues Venezuela’s 2006 building code — which was in effect when the buildings were constructed — required that short pieces of rebar, or “stirrups,” be bent to 135-degree angles in every high-rise building across La Guaira. This safeguard makes it harder for earthquakes to break or unseat the ties that reinforce beams and columns. But images captured across these five complexes (each comprised of several individually built towers) during their construction starting in 2011 and after the 2026 earthquakes show that some stirrups appeared to be bent to only 90 degrees. This difference likely violated Venezuelan building regulations, and experts say it could be the difference between a structure failing catastrophically or holding together during a severe earthquake. During strong seismic shaking, just a few improperly assembled stirrups could compromise the integrity of a beam or column, said Jeffrey Dowgala and Terrence Paret, structural engineers with expertise in earthquake resilience at Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates. Miyamoto, a structural engineer who has led post-earthquake damage assessments around the world, most recently in Venezuela, likened the stirrups defect to a wine barrel without properly assembled steel straps. Following the quakes, Miyamoto and his team of roughly 100 engineers have worked under Venezuela’s Ministry of Public Works to assess the structural integrity of surviving buildings. Venezuela’s Communications Ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Miyamoto told CNN the stirrups issue was pervasive in the rubble of buildings he assessed in La Guaira. A photograph taken during an OPPPE inspection of one construction site in March 2012 appears to show several stirrups containing the defect at the foundation of one tower in the complex known as OPPPE 27. All four towers at that site collapsed when the earthquakes hit 14 years later. Multiple photos of the same complex’s ruins following the earthquakes show that at least some of those defective stirrups were never rectified, experts said. Of more than 40 photos and videos CNN verified that specifically showed the stirrups, only a small minority were clearly bent properly. Images of at least two fallen complexes highlight another possible issue with the buildings’ rebar supports: they appear to be spaced closely but are only rarely bundled, as the 2006 code requires. To comply with the code, rebar strands must either be bundled together to act as a single unit or be separated by a gap of at least one bar diameter — and sometimes more, depending on their placement. This, too, can degrade the structural integrity of a concrete building, experts say, and underscores inconsistencies in the building techniques used. The condition of the rebar, exposed after the buildings collapsed, has also raised concerns. Footage captured after the quakes appears to show deep-seated rust in rebar in at least three collapsed OPPPE complexes; about half of collapsed buildings in this area bore signs of corrosion, Miyamoto estimates. Caraballeda’s tropical, beachfront climate could have been a factor, as well as possible impurities in the concrete used, which can eat away at the metal bars. Two construction workers who worked on one of the public housing complexes told The New York Times their team stretched materials by mixing other products into the concrete. The Times also found that the towers had no visible shear walls, and that the uniform orientation of their columns weakened these high-rises against seismic forces. Resident accounts also described issues symptomatic of poor-quality concrete. One neighbor, who often visited friends in OPPPE 26, recounted how “the floor would crack from any impact.” For her part, Quiroz doesn’t recall any similar incidents, nor did she witness any major water or sewage leaks. In October of 2025, a resident of OPPPE 26 told La Verdad that his wife was injured when a chunk of their living room ceiling dislodged and fell on her. “Luckily, she was able to cover her head and only suffered a shoulder injury,” he recalled in an interview with La Verdad de Vargas. An open question Today, several towers built by the special office remain standing — some not far from the Caraballeda complex where Quiroz’s sister died. Just over half a mile east from the Caraballeda towers stands another complex built by the special office and comprised of nearly 700 apartments. Of its seven towers, five survived this year’s twin earthquakes. They have now been evacuated and displaced residents are camping in tents outside, according to María Sánchez, a resident who spoke to CNN. It is unclear whether those buildings will be put back into use. A 2012 photo taken during construction of the complex, named OPPPE 25, shows rebar stirrups assembled with the same 90-degree bends. CNN reached out to the Venezuelan government and the office of the mayor of La Guaira, José Manuel Suárez Maldonado, but is yet to hear back. CNN’s Thomas Bordeaux and Abel Alvarado contributed to this report.

articles.title: Hiding in plain sight? Russell Brand’s conviction poses tough questions for UK entertainment industry
articles.summary: The judge presiding over Russell Brand’s criminal court case says the comedian will be handed down a lengthy prison sentence Monday after he was found guilty in a London court of raping a young fan and sexually assaulting three women.
articles.body: The judge presiding over Russell Brand’s criminal court case says the comedian will be handed down a lengthy prison sentence Monday after he was found guilty in a London court of raping a young fan and sexually assaulting three women. While that much is certain, other questions remain, including one that is worryingly familiar in the UK, a country that has seen the downfall of a host of celebrities accused of sexual offenses. How did he evade justice for so long? The 51-year-old former stand-up comedian’s conviction and the flurry of reaction from those who once moved in his orbit comes at a time of heightened debate in Britain about the toxic mix of fame, power and abuse. Britain’s Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said Sunday that sexual abuse remained a problem in the media industry. “Hand on heart I can’t say ‌to you as the ⁠culture secretary that this is not happening today and in fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is,” she told the BBC. She warned that women were often too afraid to report offenses as “speaking up has ​a very ‌heavy ​cost.” Just this week, the popular TV show Married at First Sight UK was axed following an investigation into rape allegations, according to Channel 4, at the same time as British media reported that an unnamed celebrity is attempting to block the publication of his name in relation to sexual misconduct allegations. After Brand’s guilty verdict, London’s Metropolitan Police superintendent said in a statement that as his profile grew during his acting and comedy career, “so too did his sense of entitlement.” The Met police also confirmed investigations are continuing regarding two further allegations of rape made against Brand. Prosecutors are assessing whether to bring additional charges, according to Britain’s Press Association (PA). “I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be,” senior police officer Andy Furphy said. But that statement has done little to hold back a wave of concern about the seeming immunity of some powerful figures to skirt accountability. A mix of grief and relief Responding to the verdict, British actress Sarah Solemani, who starred in the Bafta-winning sitcom “Him & Her,” said in an op-ed that Brand is finally facing justice but warned that other abusers are “still hiding in plain sight.” She said the comedy industry has “for some strange reason, brought me into the close orbit of more than your average number of sexual predators, several of whom are still merrily working.” “I had to pull a project from a company when I was informed it was common knowledge that a high-level exec was known for allegedly raping a colleague. Another famous comic had to pull a project when I informed them a legend they were working with was also an alleged rapist,” she wrote in the Guardian on Friday. Comedian Katherine Ryan, who worked with Brand on a comedy show in 2018, also responded to the verdict, saying on her podcast that she felt “grief” and “relief,” while commending the bravery of the survivors who “came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money (and) a legion of fans ready to attack them.” As well as figures within the comedy circuit, British broadcasters have also found themselves in the crossfire. After Brand’s conviction, the BBC reissued a statement about the celebrity’s controversial stint at the broadcaster in the 2000s, saying it was of “great concern to us that some people felt unable to raise concerns about Brand’s behaviour.” “We apologised to those impacted, for both the culture and failings at the time, and we reiterate that apology again today,” the BBC said. Brand’s convictions date back to 2004, 2005 and 2009, the decade when Brand moved from alternative comedy on a radically twisting path that took him to British television, Hollywood and eventually the world of podcasting and conspiracy theories. In 2006, Brand began co-hosting “The Russell Brand Show” on BBC Radio 2, a weekly Saturday night program during which he had frank, comedic and often X-rated conversations with a co-host and guests. However, the popular radio show ended abruptly two years later with Brand’s exit after the comedian and his co-host left a series of misogynistic voice messages for famed actor and “Fawlty Towers” star Andrew Sachs about his granddaughter. During a live radio segment, Brand and his then-co-presenter Jonathan Ross made lewd remarks about Brand’s relationship with Sachs’ granddaughter, Georgina Baillie, with the incident prompting several resignations and sparking a national backlash. Baillie sent her support to Brand’s victims following Thursday’s verdict while speaking about the devastating impact the BBC scandal had on her life. “Justice has been served. Although he never raped or assaulted me as I have always said, I didn’t know what happened in the privacy of the rooms that the victims and Russell were in and their evidence was compelling,” she told Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. “I now want Russell to right the wrongs.” Brand’s exposure represents the latest in a string of historic abuse investigations into former BBC stars, including sex offenders Rolf Harris and Jimmy Savile who were both staples of family television during their heyday. “There can be no place for the abuse of power. Across the industry we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else’s hand feels able to report it, that their concerns are taken seriously and that they are listened to,” a BBC spokesperson said in a statement. ‘A matter of regret for our industry’ Allegations of rape and sexual assault against Brand were made public in a joint 2023 investigation by three British media outlets – The Sunday Times, The Times and Channel 4’s “Dispatches” program. Brand has denied the allegations in the program, which related to multiple women who were not involved in the criminal trial. Esella Hawkey, the executive producer of the documentary, “Russell Brand: In Plain Sight,” said she was pleased with the verdict but added that she “would much rather these events not have happened in the first place.” Speaking about how Brand evaded justice for so long, Hawkey told CNN it can be “very difficult” for individuals to challenge “so-called talent and very big names who, you know, have a huge monetary value for the broadcasters.” “I think television and broadcasting does have a problem with dealing with that behavior and also in enabling people,” she said. “I really do hope that this is an opportunity for the industry to do some inward looking.” On Thursday, the director of news at Channel 4, Louise Compton, said “the trial heard that women involved in the criminal case came forward after seeing the Channel 4 Dispatches film,” while commending the courage of the women involved. The TV channel’s role in spotlighting the former comedian’s behaviour has not made it immune from criticism. Following the 2023 revelations, Channel 4 announced it had opened an investigation into whether people at the channel were aware of Brand’s behavior while he was engaged in programs made for the broadcaster between 2004 and 2007. The network said the investigation did not find any evidence to suggest Channel 4 employees were aware of Brand’s behavior documented in the expose, but then-CEO of Channel 4 Alex Mahon apologized over a separate allegation about Brand in 2009 that she said was not investigated as it should have been. “In my view, it is a matter of regret for our industry that repugnant behaviours were tolerated – and indeed appeared on-air – in the past,” Mahon said. articles.title: Kraków shooting that killed 6 was motivated by far-right views, authorities say
articles.summary: World leaders have paid tribute as Poland declared two national days of mourning after a shooter motivated by far-right ideologies killed six people in Kraków on Saturday, in what the country’s defense minister characterized as a “terror attack.”
articles.body: World leaders have paid tribute as Poland declared two national days of mourning after a shooter motivated by far-right ideologies killed six people in Kraków on Saturday, in what the country’s defense minister characterized as a “terror attack.” The gunman, described by officials as having “ultranationalistic” beliefs, is reported to have opened fire in Kraków’s main market square. Four women and two men were killed in the midday attack, the country’s deadliest shooting in decades, while a policeman who confronted the gunman is in critical condition. The suspect is being investigated on suspicion of murder in connection with the six deaths, Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said on X Sunday, adding that he “acted with the aim of seriously intimidating a large number of people, making this a terrorist offence.” The same suspect is facing a separate murder charge over killings in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyskie, Żurek said, a town some 93 miles northeast of Kraków where three of the man’s relatives were found dead in his home. “Establishing all the circumstances of these tragic events, determining the full sequence of the perpetrator’s actions and securing evidence are currently the priorities of the investigation,” which is being led by terror offence specialists within the prosecutor’s office, he said. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński did not name the suspect but identified him as a Polish national in his mid-20s from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyskie. He used an automatic rifle, Kierwiński said Saturday, describing him as having “ultranationalistic” views. “Everything indicates he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” he said. The suspect was shot by police at the scene and taken to the hospital around 3 p.m. local time. He remains in critical condition, regional governor Krzysztof Klęczar told a news conference Sunday. A man and two women later found dead in an apartment are believed to be the suspect’s parents and sister, according to Andrzej Fijołek, deputy inspector of Police National Headquarters. Two national days of mourning on November 8 and 9 were announced by the Interior Ministry on Sunday. Żurek, the justice minister, said on social media early on Sunday that Senior Constable Jakub Kulik “is fighting for his life in hospital” after he confronted the shooter. “One of his lungs is not functioning, and he needs every drop of blood he can get,” he posted on X. Police later said that blood banks in Kraków were full and thanked those who donated. “Senior constable Jakub Kulik and senior constable Artur Moranski are true heroes,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, referring to both policemen. Klęczar said that without “the efficient and selfless intervention” of the officers, “the number of victims could have been significantly higher.” “The condition of the two police officers remains serious,” Klęczar said Sunday, though Kierwiński later said the two men had been brought out of comas. Video posted on social media shows what appears to be an injured police officer firing at the gunman before dropping to his knees and rolling over onto his back. The officer, who did not appear to have backup nearby, is seen struggling to reload his firearm and appeared to be clutching his right arm. Four of the dead in the city center attack have been identified, though their names have not been released. They include four Polish nationals, a British national, and one non-Polish woman whose nationality has not yet been publicized, Klęczar said. All those wounded were alive on Sunday, he said, adding that 11 of the 16 injured people are Polish and two of the individuals are police officers. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the U.K. government “deeply mourns the British national and other victims” who died in the shooting. “The U.K. stands resolutely in solidarity with the people of Poland,” he said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said Saturday that his country “stands in solidarity” with neighboring Poland, calling the shooting a “shocking crime.” The U.S. State Department said it was not aware of any American citizens harmed in the violence. “The profound depth of Poland’s shock at the horror of yesterday’s appalling mass murder in Krakow is truly remarkable to behold,” U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said in a post on X. Noting how rare the incident was in a “extraordinarily safe” country like Poland, he added: “There’s something profoundly precious about being in a country where such evil remains so foreign to everyday life, where an entire nation recoils in horror at the mere thought of it, and where the depth of grief reveals the true goodness of its people.” Part of Main Market Square in Kraków and surrounding streets reopened Sunday, but cordons remain in place while police carry out forensic work, the city has said in a statement. Several makeshift memorials with flowers and candles appeared across the city on Sunday. Tourists caught up in attack Many of those caught up in the attack were tourists visiting the city. Taylor Dorfmeister, a 21-year-old American student studying in Italy who was visiting Poland, was in the square with his roommate when gunfire erupted. Dorfmeister said there was a delay before the crowd reacted and then everyone began to flee the area. He said he took shelter in a building. “We ran up the stairs in the building to hide and it was a dead end, which is when I was the most terrified since the gunshots were [loud] and near,” Dorfmeister told NBC News. It sounded to Dorfmeister like the gunfire was coming from the first floor of the building where he hid. The student from Santa Cruz, California, was “fully prepared for the worst” based on the proximity of the noise, he said. “This is it,” Dorfmeister thought. “Like, there’s nowhere to go, nowhere to hide.” Marie-Ange Collaer was visiting with her family from Brussels. “We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around,” she wrote on Facebook. “Lying on the floor in a shop like in a bad police movie whilst you hear bullets everywhere.” Collaer said her family was shaky and “quite in shock” after returning to their hotel but everyone was grateful to be alive. “We saw a few that did not make it, true horror,” she wrote. U.K. resident Neil Thaxton and his wife, Nicky, also survived the attack. “We had just walked through the main square and heard the gunshots,” Thaxton wrote on Facebook. “We thought it was fireworks then people started running, we went into a gift shop and the staff took us in the back of the shop and locked the doors and turned the lights off.”

articles.title: Dormice 'thrive' at Killerton National Trust site in Devon
articles.summary: Killerton National Trust has 100 nest boxes across its estate in Devon.
articles.body:
Habitat work and a monitoring scheme have helped hazel dormice thrive at a National Trust site, despite declines elsewhere, experts have said.

Killerton National Trust has 100 nest boxes across its estate in Devon. Rangers weigh and record details of each mouse between April and October.

The trust said the animals "continue to thrive" in the area - a sign it was "doing something right" by creating a "healthy, diverse and well-connected habitat for wildlife".

The People's Trust for Endangered Species said populations had declined by over two thirds in the UK since 2000. Experts said the decline was largely down to "habitat fragmentation".

The trust hopes the mammals, which typically weigh between 20g and 40g, will have gained enough weight to begin hibernating in the coming weeks and survive the winter ahead.

Fi Hailstone, senior ranger for the National Trust at the Killerton estate, said: "When we have warmer weather, it wakes them up and when we have wet springs, that affects their ability to forage when they do wake up.

"So having a resilient ecosystem with lots of shelter for them, lots of scrub, lots of things for them to eat [is important]."

"They love bramble, and I know that bramble has a bit of a bad reputation with a lot of gardeners," Hailstone said.

"But bramble is the life source, really. It has flowers in the spring, it has berries on it. It's also protective in terms of cover from other predators, so it's a really great place for them to nest."

When they are not hibernating, they are shy and nocturnal.

Hailstone said Devon was "a bit of a stronghold for dormice" because "there is such a strong hedge network".

"We've been monitoring our dormouse population at Killerton since 2018, and during that time, we've noticed that they are fairly stable, which does buck national trends."

Hailstone said: "We are finding them in new areas which indicates them spreading across the estate.

"We think this is because we're planting a lot more hedges, a lot more trees."

"We might be planting lots of woodland now, which is great, but we won't see the effects of that for dormice for another 100 or so years," Hailstone added.

"It's really important to manage the woodlands that we already have in a positive way."

Anyone who finds a dormouse in the winter is urged not to pick it up but to alert the RSPCA or local animal shelter.

articles.title: Poland mourns six killed in attack as authorities launch ‘terrorism’ probe
articles.summary: ‘Terrorism’ investigation launched after government officials say suspect likely influenced by far-right ideology.
articles.body:
Poland has begun two days of national mourning after an armed man killed six people in central Krakow, as the national prosecutor’s office opened a “terrorism” investigation.

The 24-year-old Polish suspect opened fire on Saturday in the heart of Krakow’s historic city centre. A British national was among those killed, according to police, and nationals from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia were among the 15 wounded, authorities told the PAP news agency.

Three more bodies were later found at the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, about 150km (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. Police said they were his parents and a sister.

The suspect was also wounded during police action and is in critical condition in hospital.

Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office said on social media on Sunday it had “launched an investigation today into yesterday’s attack in Krakow”, adding it was probing “the killing of six people … using a firearm, and the attempted murder of many others, including police officers, this act constituting a terrorist offence”.

Daniel Prokopowicz, a spokesperson for the office, said it was “highly likely” that the killings in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski and Krakow were carried out by the same person, but that investigations were ongoing.

According to media reports, the suspect, Michal O, had a valid gun licence and no prior criminal record.

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski stated the attacker was influenced by far-right and ultranationalist ideologies and views.

Meanwhile, Krakow’s main market square and ⁠the surrounding streets remained closed on Sunday, with police allowing only essential service workers.

Many nearby cafes were closed and flags ⁠at the city hall were at half-mast. Mourners placed candles in several locations in the area.

The traditional hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s church on the square was suspended for 12 hours to commemorate the dead, the first time this has happened since 1939, the Polish Press Agency reported.

articles.title: Pope Leo heads to Milei’s Argentina as tensions loom over austerity, Iran
articles.summary: MONTEVIDEO — Pope Leo heads on Sunday to Argentina on the second leg ​of a 12-day tour across South America, where the first U.S.-born pope will give a closely watched speech to Argentine ‌President Javier Milei, a libertarian seen as a close ally of Donald Trump.
articles.body: MONTEVIDEO — Pope Leo heads on Sunday to Argentina on the second leg ​of a 12-day tour across South America, where the first U.S.-born pope will give a closely watched speech to Argentine ‌President Javier Milei, a libertarian seen as a close ally of Donald Trump. The address may underscore tensions between the Vatican and Milei, whose austerity agenda has been criticized by the Church for hitting the poorest most and who has strongly supported the Iran war, which Leo has criticized, to Trump’s ire. Leo, on an ambitious three-country tour through November 17, is arriving ​in Argentina from Uruguay, where he urged South American countries to tackle regional issues together and set an example for the value of patient ​diplomacy over conflict. The 71-year-old pontiff, who is making one of the most intense foreign trips of a Catholic leader in ⁠decades less than a month after undergoing lung cancer surgery, is the first Catholic leader to visit Argentina since 1987 and will tour four cities until ​Wednesday. Speech will be carefully parsed Milei swept to power in 2023 after a run of center-left Peronist rule, campaigning with a chainsaw as a symbol ​of the deep cuts to state spending he pledged to make to shore up the country’s finances. Leo, who addresses national governments on each of his foreign visits, usually speaks in careful, diplomatic language but has emerged as a more forceful voice on the world stage recently, decrying the direction of global leadership. He is not expected to directly criticize Milei by name but ​may refer to national policies or international events in remarks that will be carefully parsed by political observers. “Any interventions by Leo, particularly on poverty, ​the limits of markets or confrontational political rhetoric, could be read as implicit criticism of Milei and amplify existing opposition to the government’s approach,” said Nicolas Watson, a managing ‌director at ⁠advisory firm Teneo. Milei has defended his austerity as the only way to bring inflation under control. Under his economic campaign, annual inflation has fallen from over 200% to 33%. But surveys show his popularity has slipped ahead of elections next year as Argentines contend with subsidy cuts, public-sector layoffs and business closures linked to squeezed household budgets. Pope’s visit highlights the marginalized Over his 18-month papacy, Leo has forcefully warned about the risks of artificial intelligence, urged world leaders to ​treat immigrants more humanely, and called for ​action to address climate change, appeals ⁠that have put him at odds with Trump and other right-wing leaders. Fortunato Mallimaci, a sociologist at Argentina’s Conicet research agency, said Leo’s visit to Argentina will create a sense of unity and energy among those who feel excluded ​by Milei’s economic program. The pope’s itinerary in Argentina includes visits to a care center for people with disabilities ​and a prison, underscoring ⁠his focus on highlighting groups that are often marginalized. Jorge Silanes, religious director of the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione care center that will welcome the pope on Monday, said the visit carried added significance because spending cuts have reduced disability benefits while poverty remains widespread. Milei was known for piling insults on Leo’s predecessor, Francis, ⁠an Argentine who never ​came home during his 12-year papacy. Despite calling Francis “an imbecile,” Milei eventually sought to repair ​relations and visited the late pope at the Vatican. “Milei doesn’t win anything by fighting with (Leo),” said Veronica Gimenez Beliveau, a sociologist at the University of Buenos Aires. “He could gain in showing an ​orderly country and administration,” she said.

articles.summary: At least 21 people were killed after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, with only one survivor rescued so far, authorities said on
articles.body: At least 21 people were killed after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, with only one survivor rescued so far, authorities said on Sunday.The Senegalese interior ministry said 21 bodies had been recovered by Saturday evening and search and rescue operations were continuing for possible survivors. The death toll was provisional, it added, without specifying how many people were aboard the boat.The boat capsized off Kebemer, about 180 km north of Dakar, near the Loumpoul dunes in northwestern Senegal, according to local media reports.Most of the victims were reportedly from the Leona and Thieppe districts in the Kebemer department, the Le Soleil newspaper reported.The latest tragedy adds to the toll of migrants attempting the perilous Atlantic crossing from West Africa to Spain's Canary Islands. Thousands have died in recent years while attempting the journey. At least 635 people died along the route in the first five months of this year, according to migrant rights group Walking Borders.The incident came a day after Senegalese authorities intercepted 142 migrants aboard another small boat allegedly attempting to reach Spain. The group included 23 women, two babies and two other children, and comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.The Senegalese government said it was determined to combat people-smuggling networks, including through stronger cooperation with neighbouring countries.Meanwhile, authorities on Spain's Canary Island of El Hierro declared an emergency on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals. More than 3,300 people had reached the island aboard around 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.Senegal, Mauritania and Morocco have stepped up maritime patrols near departure points, pushing migrant boats further south towards the coasts of Gambia, Guinea-Bissau and Guinea, lengthening an already hazardous crossing.You use AI every day. articles.title: New Zealanders won’t know for weeks who won the election as neither side secures clear victory
articles.summary: WELLINGTON, New Zealand — New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday’s election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side.
articles.body: WELLINGTON, New Zealand — New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday’s election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side. The tightest vote in years delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties which have long dominated New Zealand politics, Christopher Luxon’s center-right National party and center-left Labour led by Chris Hipkins, as voters threw more support behind minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. On Saturday’s numbers, minor parties would enter negotiations for a governing deal with leverage to extract deeper policy concessions from a weakened National or Labour. The near-deadlock was partly produced because voters, apparently weary of New Zealand’s economic woes and apathetic about both Luxon and Hipkins, chose to propel a new entrant group to Parliament for the first time in years. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government. Wong’s pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering had on Saturday’s results secured seven seats for Opportunity — enough to frustrate both left and right in a simple path to power. It was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago. The conservative bloc has a simpler route to victory, but results could change Other winners were harder to identify and on Sunday, “who won the election 2026” was the top trending Google search in New Zealand. So unclear was the result that parties won’t begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on Nov. 27, confirming the exact number of seats they’ve won. With 2.8 million ballots counted on election night, the conservative incumbent government led by Luxon’s National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power — by just one seat. However, Luxon didn’t claim victory, instead striking a note of cautious optimism that he could negotiate a second term in power. Speaking to reporters Sunday, Luxon blamed public dissatisfaction on global shocks which have buffeted New Zealand’s trade-based economy, noting that other incumbent governments worldwide have faced voters’ rancor over living costs. Yet his opponent Hipkins, who was turfed from office in 2023 largely over discontent about the same economic issues, didn’t appear to benefit on Saturday. The left-wing bloc appeared to fall short of a majority but was still hopeful it could triumph — though that seemed a more remote prospect. Electoral officials were due on Sunday to begin counting nearly 400,000 so-called special votes, including from New Zealanders who live abroad, a process expected to take three weeks. Those ballots have historically granted an additional seat or two in Parliament to left-wing parties, which could snatch the current razor-thin majority from the right, although such an outcome would likely leave the left struggling to form a majority too. If a government can’t be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote. Incumbent Luxon urges people to ‘calm down’ “I think everyone’s over politics so let’s all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks,” Luxon told reporters on Sunday. He will lead a caretaker government until an outcome is reached. Luxon suggested that National had a viable path to power and boasted that it had secured more seats in Parliament than any other group. However, Saturday night was bleak for his party. Several of National’s most senior lawmakers would exit politics on results so far, including the ministers of finance and defense, the speaker of parliament, and the attorney general. With the party’s traditional governing partners winning increased support, Luxon faces a more strident list of policy demands to secure their backing. Libertarian ACT won 13 seats and populist New Zealand First won 12. Both are led by canny veteran politicians, and detractors of Luxon, a former business executive who entered politics in 2020, said his dealings with them in the three years since he took office had highlighted his political inexperience. The vote was a slap for both major parties New Zealanders don’t vote for prime ministers. Instead they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and another for the candidate they want as their local representative. The country has one house of Parliament and no states, so the central government holds ultimate sway over New Zealand’s direction. Governments in the South Pacific nation of 5.6 million people are elected every three years. National won just 29.21% of the preferred party vote as of Sunday, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races. Luxon, who unusually faced two separate confidence votes among his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day. However, Labour also won just 29.36% of the party vote, a result that appeared to suggest a second election defeat for career politician Hipkins. Despite winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour has secured only 36 seats on numbers so far because they won fewer local races. Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The environmentally-focused Greens won 16 seats and Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five. The total number of seats in New Zealand’s Parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats required for a majority. Luxon’s conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties. However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted. Even if the final tally boosted the left bloc’s seats slightly, Hipkins would apparently need support from newcomer Wong to govern. Before the election, Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Wong. He sidestepped questions on Sunday about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.

articles.title: Iran executes three men for 'armed unrest' after January protests
articles.summary: It is claimed Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were part of anti-government protests earlier this year.
articles.body:
Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.

Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim reported.

The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States.

The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February.

The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel.

However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.

Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups".

The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas.

Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.

Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested.

Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.

The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker Türk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties .

In August, Türk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.

Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.

The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

articles.title: Far-right wingnuts storm Diwali fest in Seattle after lights go out on MAGA
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: A celebration of light, colour, diversity, and religious pluralism in Seattle turned into a brief demonstration of
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: A celebration of light, colour, diversity, and religious pluralism in Seattle turned into a brief demonstration of America's darker side when two far-right activists gate-crashed the festivities carrying placards demanding the deportation of "dot heads" and warning of a “Hindu takeover of Christian America.”Jake Lang and Thomas Allen apparently didn't get the memo that Diwali is a celebration of the triumph of good over evil. They turned up at a local Diwali celebration with American flags determined to underscore the evil part. They were eventually escorted out of the Seattle Center Armory after a scuffle, but not before Lang, who seems to have a particular talent for turning provocation into publicity, claimed that he and Allen had been assaulted by "Antifa and Hindus," while blaming Hindus for the Republicans' electoral disaster in Texas. ""Hindus flipped Texas blue. F**k them," he complained, planting the idea in some heads that they should now be celebrating Krishna Jayanti in Texas.Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, whose Congressional district includes Seattle, condemned the disruption, saying she is beyond disgusted by this vile and racist display. “Diwali is an important holiday and our community should feel safe to celebrate it. This hateful display has no place in our city or this country,” the lawmaker, who has herself faced racist attacks asking her to go back to India, said. Suhag Shukla, executive director of the Hindu American Foundation, said she’d “laugh these losers off as clowns looking for some instagram likes if their fellow white nationalist hadn’t almost shot up a Hindu temple in Chicago.”Indeed, Lang is a familiar figure in violent far-right activism, coming to prominence after participating in the January 6 attack on the US Capitol. He was accused of assaulting police officers with a baseball bat and a stolen riot shield and faced 11 federal counts, including assaulting law enforcement officers, before he was pardoned by President Trump along with other people prosecuted for offenses connected to January 6. articles.title: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
articles.summary: Wreaths are laid as 10,000 armed forces veterans, including 12 from World War Two, pay tribute in central London.
articles.body:
King Charles III led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who had died in conflict.

On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.

That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".

Meanwhile, the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham attended for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.

And for the first time, the leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, had enough MPs in Parliament to qualify to lay a wreath alongside other major party leaders.

The Prince of Wales and the Princess Royal were among royals in attendance, along with military chiefs, senior politicians, diplomats and faith leaders, watched by big crowds squeezed behind railings along Whitehall.

Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales watched from a balcony above the Cenotaph in the Foreign Office.

Among the flags on the roof of that Whitehall building was the Ukrainian blue and yellow. It went up when Russia invaded and four years later it is now visibly frayed - a reminder of the length of that war and of current threats.

At 11:00 GMT, as the first strike of Big Ben echoed from the nearby Houses of Parliament, the big two-minute silence filled the usually frenetic streets, before the playing of the Last Post.

The King had his eyes closed, the crowds in Whitehall stopped for their own thoughts, in a rare moment of calm in the capital.

The poignant parade past the Cenotaph included representatives of about 340 different military and civilian groups, from the Royal Naval Association and the Royal Marines Association to Transport for London and the Royal National Lifeboat Institute.

Alongside those marching were flotillas of disability scooters and families helping veterans in wheelchairs.

Those who took part in WW2 are now increasingly frail - and there were 12 participants in the march-past compared to 20 last year. The oldest participant this year was aged 105.

Taking part for the first time was 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who had been part of the Land Army that had helped to feed the country at war.

She had joined the Land Army in 1940 as a 16-year-old, having lied about her age, and worked on a farm in Leicestershire.

"I feel very honoured to be taking part in the parade and to represent the Land Girls. I'm very excited, although a little apprehensive as I don't quite know what to expect," she said.

"I think it will be a very emotional day, bringing back memories of all those who didn't return home. It will be lovely to be there and remember them."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the annual event was a time to "reflect on the selflessness and courage it takes to commit your life to protecting others".

He earlier announced that he wanted to tackle the problem of homelessness among ex-service personnel to "ensure that any veteran sleeping rough is offered appropriate accommodation before Christmas".

Mark Atkinson, the director general of the Royal British Legion, said: "As we come together on Remembrance Sunday, we pay tribute to all those who have served and sacrificed, from generations past to those still serving today."

For more than a century, this national Remembrance event has been held around the Cenotaph.

The monument was built as a focal point for honouring those who had fought and died in World War One, including those who had no grave, and as a place to mourn for those families who might not be able to visit war cemeteries overseas.

The word "cenotaph" means "empty tomb" in Greek and it was designed by the architect Sir Edwin Lutyens in a simple, austere style, with no sense of triumphalism and with almost no decoration.

The monument had been originally built in 1919 as a temporary, plaster and wood structure. But it proved so popular with the public that it was replaced in 1920 with a permanent version, in the same design but in stone.

It was opened at 11:00 on 11 November 1920 by King George V. His great-grandson, Charles, was there again, on an overcast morning 106 years later, to continue paying respect.

articles.title: US task force to cut off Iran’s transport of advanced weapons: What we know
articles.summary: As fears of an escalation grow, Washington announces ‘Task Force Iron Gate’.
articles.body:
As the threat of renewed war grows, Washington is expanding efforts to choke Tehran’s military supply networks, including through Task Force Iron Gate – a unit targeting land routes and the Caspian Sea.

With it, the US military ⁠⁠⁠⁠is trying to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Saturday.

The same day, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced ambitious plans for underground complexes capable of sustaining missile and drone production under bombardment. That announcement came amid reports of ongoing construction near Iranian missile bases, based on satellite imagery and previous claims by Tehran that US strikes failed to destroy its underground facilities.

Here’s what we know about the US task force:

Task Force Iron Gate will aim to find out where “weapons systems are coming in, how they could potentially be cut off” and how “Iran is transporting its energy”, Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defence secretary for the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.

It expands on the US blockade of Iranian ports to cover Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea and will reportedly be run by 20 civilian and military personnel.

Iran shares borders with seven countries – Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan Turkiye and Turkmenistan.

Based in Tampa, Florida, the unit will coordinate with other US government agencies “on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea”, CENTCOM said. Task Force Iron Gate will reinforce “the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea”, CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.

If US President Donald Trump ramps up the war, there will likely be attacks on this “series of targets”, said Mulroy.

“Unlike Operation Epic Fury , which primarily (focused) on military targets, I think these targets will be focused on economic and infrastructure targets, as part of this comprehensive plan to cut the regime off from its ability to fight and ability to fund itself,” Mulroy said. “It’s primarily a coordination body that’s looking for how the US can increase its economic strangulation strategy by going after the ground routes as they’ve already covered a majority of the maritime routes.”

How has Iran responded to CENTCOM’s announcement?

The IRGC dismissed the US military plan as “just a play on words”.

“The Americans cannot achieve their goal through this, which is to apply severe economic pressure to collapse and disintegrate the Iranian economy,” said IRGC spokesman Sardar Mohebi, as reported by the Fars news agency.

Washington previously “claimed that Iran will suffer an economic collapse within two weeks, but we witnessed that this did not happen”, he added.

Is the task force a response to reports of Russia-Iran weapons ties?

While CENTCOM’s announcement did not explicitly identify Iran’s weapons trade with Russia, analysts say the unit could be seen as an attempt to disrupt supply networks that include Russian connections.

US media have reported that Russia has sent drone components and explosives to Iran via the Caspian Sea. There are also claims that Russian technology could be helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles.

Mahjoob Zweiri, a professor of contemporary history and politics at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that reports of military equipment imported via Russia are a “real concern” for the United States.

The task force therefore could “cause a confrontation with Russia”, he said.

Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut and a non-resident senior fellow at the Arab Center in Washington, said of the new unit: “The US really doesn’t quite know what to do about Iran as we’ve seen, and it’s doing things off the cuff” – a strategy that has led to little success.

Can the US really choke off Iran’s supply lines?

Khouri pointed to Iran’s history as a trading nation for thousands of years as evidence that the US mission is near impossible.

“There’s an enormous web of contacts that Iran has had for thousands of years with traders and partners and allies all over the region, especially in Asia – it’s virtually impossible for the US to seal off every one,” he said.

While the US can impose a blockade or sanctions on Iran, it cannot control the behaviour of everyone from the Russians, to the Chinese, to the Emiratis and beyond, said the analyst.

“There are people all over the region who have links with Iran, some very close, some just commercial,” he said.

A lot of the materials that go into Iran’s weapons systems are bought from some other countries, – some even from the US or Europeans – and then they are channelled through companies in Asia, Khouri added.

Could this change the course of the war?

Former Trump aide and top counterterrorism official Joe Kent, who resigned in March due to the US’s war on Iran, said the new task force is an attempt by CENTCOM to subvert ongoing diplomatic efforts.

“This is CENTCOM inviting Iran to escalate while the vice president is attempting to negotiate with the Iranians,” Kent posted on X. “This is, as CENTCOM calls it, ‘policy by CONOP’, when the military finds a way to subvert the White House without blatantly disobeying the President, by taking actions that will ensure a war escalates or perpetuates.”

According to The Wall Street Journal, CENTCOM chief Cooper is among the many officials, alongside Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing Trump to renew attacks on Iran.

The task force may also just be symbolic because the US has no military presence on the Caspian Sea, said Zweiri.

“America has no access to the sea, unless some of the neighbouring countries like Azerbaijan or Armenia or others collaborate [with them] … And they’re not collaborating on this because they don’t want to upset Russia,” he said. “It will require … troops on the ground, and this is unlikely to happen.”

Zweiri also said that the Caspian Sea’s contribution to Iran’s economy is just 11 percent, so the task force’s actions won’t have much negative impact on Tehran.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify this figure but the Caspian Sea accounts for only a fraction of Iran’s overall maritime trade, according to the Soufan Center based in New York City.

articles.title: Giorgia Meloni blames pro-Russian hackers for leaking foreign minister’s personal data to dark web
articles.summary: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Saturday blamed pro-Russian hackers for the leaking her foreign minister’s personal data onto the dark web. After foreign minister Antonio Tajani said he was targeted by hackers over his support for Ukraine, Meloni said separately that the “sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious…
articles.body:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Saturday blamed pro-Russian hackers for the leaking her foreign minister’s personal data onto the dark web.

After foreign minister Antonio Tajani said he was targeted by hackers over his support for Ukraine, Meloni said separately that the “sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination.”

“Of equal concern is the circulation of false images, which have also been shared by members of the opposition,” she said in an official statement . “Freedom of expression must never become a breeding ground for disinformation.”

Tajani said “cybercriminals” had exposed his personal data to the dark web and were “looking for more information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation,” as well as targeting his family. He noted that the leaks had been happening for days, targeting his family too.

“My response is very simple: I will not be intimidated in any way,” he wrote on the social platform X . “I will continue working to defend my ministry and Italy, and I will keep strengthening ties and cooperation with our allies so that we can protect ourselves together.”

Meloni’s government holds close ties to that of Ukraine, with President Volodymyr Zelensky writing on X last month that he and the prime minister have a “very good relationship.”

“They receive feedback from us on which Italian-made and European-made weapons work and which do not, and what we have improved technologically,” he said on X , sharing part of an interview with the Italian news outlet Corriere della Sera. “We share all of this with Italian manufacturers.”

Meloni has slammed the European Union for giving the impression of being “all over the place” when addressing the Russia-Ukraine war, Politico reported . She has called for the European Union to promote someone who can take a prominent role in future negotiations between Ukraine and Russia.

“I’m convinced that we all realize how, by projecting the image of a Europe that’s all over the place, we’re doing nothing but serving the interests of those who want this war to continue,” she told the outlet. “And I think this is unacceptable, given that human lives and the future of our security are at stake.”

Zelensky said last week that the U.S. could provide his country with further assistance after Democrats won sweeping victories in the 2026 midterm elections. He also said he had conversations with President Trump’s top envoys for negotiations, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, ahead of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. scheduled in Abu Dhabi next week.

articles.title: Utah tested connected snowploughs on five winter corridors; equipped routes recorded larger reported crash-rate reductions, up to 3.87 versus 1.82 on matched routes, but the study could not establish that the technology caused the difference
articles.summary: Utah's trial of connected snowploughs on winter corridors has shown a significant reduction in crash rates compared to matched routes, highlighting the potential of vehicle-to-everything (V2X) technology for safer winter travel.
articles.body: Anyone who has crawled through a snowy morning commute probably knows how one red light can slow things down, even for the trucks sent to clear the road. Utah decided to try a fix. According to the US Department of Transportation’s ITS Deployment Evaluation, the state tested connected snowploughs on 5 winter corridors around Salt Lake City. Equipped routes showed greater reductions in crash rates, up to 3.87, than matched routes, 1.82, both measured in crashes per million vehicle miles travelled.How does a snowplough ask for a green light?The test used vehicle-to-everything (V2X) technology. Vehicles use wireless technology to communicate brief messages to their surroundings. V2X devices were installed in snowploughs, while roadside devices were put up near traffic signals along test routes. When a plough reached a junction, it could ask to have the signal changed in its favour. Engineers call this signal preemption, and the same idea is used for emergency vehicles. Researchers at Brigham Young University studied the test for the Utah Department of Transportation and published their findings in a July 2022 report.What the test found The field trial ran from October 2019 to March 2020. Each of the five equipped corridors was paired with similar roads without the technology, and the data was collected on the same snow days on both. The report matched the pairs on traffic levels, lane layout, direction, and location, although there were some differences that remained. Ploughs asked for a green light on more than half of the approaches to a junction. More than 80% of these requests were granted by signals. This indicated that the system was used frequently and worked as intended, the report says. Traffic on the equipped routes also moved at speeds closer to the speed limit than did traffic on the other routes.Crashes were the highlight of this report. The report compared the snow seasons of 2018-2019 and 2019-2020. In most cases, equipped roads saw a greater decrease in crashes, by up to 3.87, as compared to the matched roads that saw a decrease of 1.82. The crashes without injury but only property damage decreased by 22% on equipped roads during the two seasons. These types of crashes increased by 7% on roads without the technology. On the equipped roads, crash severity thus moved in the same direction as the overall crash rate.Why the results need careful reading The numbers are encouraging, but they don't prove that technology alone is responsible for the decline. The study added crash analysis after the original plan. The authors say some data sets had little data, so statistical significance was unclear. They also note their findings do not account for the full benefits of the system. The weather, the traffic, and driver behaviour all change from one winter to the next. The speeds of the ploughs themselves didn't change, partly due to differences in snowfall and how fast the ploughs can go. Snowplough drivers also anecdotally reported that ploughs stopped less often and that the system was a help overall.What it means for winter roads There's reason to worry about winter crashes. The research the team reviewed found crashes were more likely the longer it had been since a plough last passed, so keeping ploughs moving matters. Utah’s test hints at a possible benefit, and the authors recommend more research. The test used a radio standard known as dedicated short-range communications. The US Federal Communications Commission has since turned its attention to cellular V2X, the report says. For now, Utah’s field test offers a measured early glimpse into how connected snowploughs could help make winter travel safer.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 1 killed and 3 wounded in shootings on Winston-Salem State University campus
articles.summary: One person has died and three others were wounded after two separate shootings on Winston-Salem State University’s campus on Saturday.
articles.body: One person has died and three others were wounded after two separate shootings on Winston-Salem State University’s campus on Saturday. Police said at a press conference early Sunday morning that investigations were in their “very preliminary” stages, without giving details on any arrests or suspects. “What we can tell you is campus is secure. The surrounding community is secure,” said Jason Swaim, assistant chief of the Field Services Bureau for the Winston-Salem Police Department. Swaim added that investigators were working to determine whether the two shootings were connected. “Our condolences go out to the families, to the friends, and anyone who witnessed this,” he said, adding extra police officers would be present on the North Carolina university’s campus in the coming days. Police received the call at around 9.45 p.m. local time. Saturday was homecoming game day at the historically black university, with the WSSU Rams facing the Fayetteville State Broncos earlier in the day. “Homecoming is traditionally a time of celebration and connection,” Swaim said. Emergency services audio obtained by NBC News showed officers reporting one victim suffered a gunshot wound to the head. Another recording showed an officer calling for a second ambulance. Remaining homecoming activities scheduled for Sunday were canceled, including an event at the Emmanuel Baptist Church, according to a statement from Winston-Salem State University Chancellor Bonita J. Brown. Brown expressed her condolences to the family of the deceased victims and said she was praying for the recovery of those who were injured. She also acknowledged that members of the campus community “may have witnessed or experienced things that no one should have to endure.” She urged people to utilize the university’s counseling services and continue to follow police instructions as the investigation in the shootings continued. “Throughout our history, Winston-Salem State University has faced challenges, but we have always found strength in one another,” Brown wrote. “That is what it means to be part of the Ramily and to be Ram strong.”

articles.title: An eight-site field test across five US cities recorded 73% fewer vehicles in the “dilemma zone” and 82% fewer red-light violations; crashes were 9% lower, but the difference was not statistically significant
articles.summary: A five-city field test demonstrates that advanced signal control systems drastically reduce vehicles in dilemma zones and red-light violations, leading to enhanced road safety and fewer crashes.
articles.body: You see the light turn yellow and have a split second to decide: brake hard or keep going. Most drivers know that doubt well. The Federal Highway Administration report, ‘Field Evaluation of Detection Control System,’ tested a smarter signal in a five-city field test. The study found 73% fewer vehicles caught in the intersection’s “dilemma zone” and 82% fewer red-light violations. Crashes were down by 9%, but that number needs a careful reading. The test didn't just cover one intersection; it was eight sites in four states.Why the yellow light is a problem The dilemma zone is the stretch of road right before the intersection. Here, drivers are usually unsure if they should stop or proceed when the signal changes to yellow. The problem is discussed in the FHWA report, which says this doubt can cause rear-end, left-turn, and sideswipe crashes. It also notes that over several years, about 21% of road deaths in the US occurred at the intersections. About 50% of severe injuries have also been recorded at intersections. Older signals tried to help. They held the light green until the road ahead was clear. However, a 2002 Texas Transportation Institute (TTI) report found a problem. On busy roads, a clear gap rarely comes. Then the green runs for its maximum time and ends anyway, which can increase the risk of a rear-end crash.How the smarter signal decides The system in the test is a detection control system (D-CS). The road has sensors that measure the vehicle's speed and length as it arrives, lane by lane. It responds to real traffic, one vehicle at a time. It treats the dilemma zone as part of the road between six and two seconds of travel time from the stop line. The software then predicts when each car or truck will enter and exit that zone. It waits for the best time to kill the green and rechecks its plan every half second. It factors in how many vehicles are in the zone and how many are queued up on the crossing road. It also tries to avoid changing the light while a truck is in the zone. The FHWA specifies that D-CS is intended for isolated intersections on high-speed roads of 45 mph or higher.What the five-city test found The study was conducted by researchers from the Texas Transportation Institute from 2008 through 2012. They used 8 locations in Florida, Illinois, Louisiana, and Texas. These locations were near Fort Lauderdale, Peoria, New Orleans, San Antonio, and Waco. The researchers compared traffic data before and after the activation of D-CS. The one-hour data showed that there were 82% fewer red-light running violations and 73% fewer vehicles in the dilemma zone. There were also 51% fewer max-outs. A max-out is basically when the green light runs to its full limit. As for crashes, the team used state records for approximately five years before and two years after the installation. For comparison, similar intersections without D-CS were used. The number of cases was small, so angle and rear-end crashes were combined. Together, they fell by 9%.What the numbers do and do not showThe biggest differences were seen in the red light and dilemma zone results. They record risky moments, not actual crashes. The 9% drop in crashes is smaller and less certain. By the report’s own measure, it was not statistically significant at the 95% level. That means some of it could be down to luck. However, the authors found supporting evidence for D-CS improving safety. The government was also looking for ways to encourage signal makers to add the system. Earlier TTI work showed equal or fewer delays and fewer red-light runners at two Texas intersections. However, D-CS was built for isolated high-speed junctions. The results should not be stretched to every crossing in a busy city around the world.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two trains collide in Egypt, killing four people and injuring dozens more, authorities say
articles.summary: At least four people have been killed and nearly 90 injured after two trains collided in Egypt, the health ministry says.
articles.body: At least four people have been killed and nearly 90 injured after two trains collided in Egypt, the health ministry says. Several carriages were derailed after one train collided with the rear of another between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Giza, near the capital Cairo, the Egyptian National Railways Authority said in a statement. Dozens of ambulances were dispatched to transport the injured to nearby hospitals, while cranes were deployed to remove the wreckage after traffic on the railroad was disrupted, Egyptian authorities said. The Egyptian railway system, the oldest in Africa and the Middle East, has a long history of deadly accidents, including when a train lost control while approaching the main station in Ramses, igniting a fire that killed 25 people. Another in 2017 occurred on the way to Alexandria, when a train derailed and collided head-on with another train, killing more than 40 people. This story has been updated.

articles.body: CAIRO — At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, authorities said. The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 32 miles south of Cairo, when a train traveling to the southwestern Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the Transportation Ministry. One of the trains derailed, it said, but did not specify which. The Health Ministry said at least four people were killed and 88 others were wounded. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.There were 72 ambulances deployed to the scene to help transport victims to three different hospitals in the area, according to the health ministry. Three of the victims died at local hospitals while one was declared dead at the scene of the crash. Al-Ayyat is located near the Nile River in the south of Giza, which is the province that is famous for being home to Egypt’s ancient pyramids. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a social media post that he ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable. Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said. Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.
