articles.title: Brooklyn cut Prospect Park West from three traffic lanes to two and added a protected bike path; speeding fell from 74% of vehicles to 20%, while injury crashes fell 63%
articles.summary: Discover how Brooklyn's transformation of Prospect Park West from three lanes to two with a protected bike path has drastically reduced speeding and injury crashes, improving overall safety for pedestrians and cyclists.
articles.body: In June 2010, Brooklyn changed one of its busiest park-edge avenues. Prospect Park West, which runs alongside Prospect Park in Park Slope, went from three moving lanes to two and the free space became a two-way protected bicycle path with a 3-foot parking lane buffer. The New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) tracked what happened next and presented the results to Community Board 6 in January 2011 in the Prospect Park West Bicycle Path and Traffic Calming Update. Two figures from NYC DOT’s January 2011 presentation travel widely: speeding fell from 74% of vehicles to 20% and injury crashes fell by 63%. Both come from narrow measurement windows.Speeding fell from 74% to 20% on one blockThe speed figures come from NYC DOT radar readings on the block between 5th and 6th Streets, so they do not represent speeds for all vehicles on the avenue. Before the redesign, an average of 74% of vehicles on that block exceeded 30 mph, or roughly three in four. The average row in the update put the share of vehicles over 30 mph at 20% after the redesign, with average speed dropping from 33.8 mph to 26.6 mph. There was a discrepancy between the two sets of ‘after’ data; however, at the morning peak hour, the figure was 11% in July and 22% in October, while in the evening, it went from 23% to 14%.Injury crashes from 5.3 to 2 per six monthsThe crash data came from NYPD records for the stretch between Grand Army Plaza and Bartel Pritchard Square, as cited in the update. The comparison set the July to December average of 2007, 2008 and 2009 against a single period, July to December 2010. Total crashes were down 16% and crashes that caused injuries were down 63%. A January 2012 NYC DOT presentation for a Transportation Research Board workshop showed the raw numbers: an average of 5.3 injury crashes per six months before the project and 2 after. It’s quite a low base when compared to just six months; hence the percentage seems to be higher when compared to the actual reduction in accidents.The above-mentioned study adds that injuries to all street users fell 21%. The study further indicates that prior to the intervention, an accident was twice as likely to contain an injury (18% vs 8%). NYPD did not report any injuries sustained by pedestrians after the intervention.Traffic held steady while weekday cycling nearly tripled The removal of one lane didn’t create any bottlenecks on the avenue. Peak-hour traffic counted on Prospect Park West at Carroll Street rose 5% in the morning (from 1,055 to 1,109 vehicles) and 2% in the evening (from 991 to 1,010 vehicles), the same pattern recorded. Weekday commute times remained the same; vehicle and cyclist counts indicated an increase of 13% in the morning and 9% in the evening. The situation was much different when it came to cycling. Weekday cycling between 3rd and 5th Streets rose 190%, but that figure came from comparing the average of four counts taken from August to November 2010 with a single count from June 2009. Sidewalk cycling volume decreased from 46% to 3%.Citywide data gives context, not a second countMaking Safer Streets, a separate report from the same agency, published in November 2013, compared crash data before and after street projects completed over seven years. There were drops in injury crashes, ranging between 12% and 88% for different streets with different designs based on three years of before data versus two to three years of after data. Among the projects listed, Bowne Street in Queens, which saw a three-to-two-lane design and safety islands for pedestrians, saw a 23% reduction in injury crashes. Prospect Park West is not in this list, thus making this report an excellent context for the park, rather than an analysis for the project. On having fewer lanes, the report argues that a street with many vague lanes may be congested by vehicles, engaging in double parking and turning movements in the lanes intended for through movement, hence the need to give the movement its place. On cycling, the report noted a 72% drop since 2000 in the average risk of serious injury to cyclists in the city, while bike trips nearly tripled. articles.title: Democrats won big on Election Day. But can they agree on AI?
articles.summary: Democrats campaigned on concerns about AI and data centers, but competing priorities and opposition from the Trump administration could complicate efforts to enact new regulations.
articles.body: Democrats across the country who swept into power amid growing voter skepticism about AI and data centers are now reckoning with knotty discussions about how to tackle AI regulation and which technological impacts deserve their attention first, according to AI experts, strategists and legislators themselves. Dusted with confetti and batting away Election Day balloons, midterm victors touched on everything from data centers — Sen.-elect Chris Pappas of New Hampshire railed against the facilities that “harm our communities and our well-being” — to healthcare, as Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota committed to restricting the use of AI systems in insurance decisions. The renewed calls for AI regulation are at odds with President Donald Trump’s insistence that Congress must limit AI-focused regulation or risk hampering American AI innovation. Trump has repeatedly referred to AI as a “golden goose” and data centers as sound economic investments. It is unclear whether Tuesday’s results could create a new opening for meaningful bipartisan AI legislation — with representatives mindful of voters’ AI hawkishness — or instead result in messy infighting within the Democratic Party, Congress and Washington. “Every Democrat in the House I’m speaking to wants to see AI regulation,” said incoming representative Scott Wiener, who pioneered California’s state-level regulation about AI and will represent San Francisco. “There may be different ideas about what that should be, but I think there’s broad support to take action.” Some Democrats, like Ohio’s Sherrod Brown, have focused their attention on data centers, often viewed as the physical manifestation of nebulous AI worries and which have stressed electrical grids and water supplies in some areas. “I do not work for data centers,” he said Tuesday night in a state that has one of the highest concentrations of the facilities in the country. Others, like re-elected Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, have also highlighted the technology’s catastrophic risks. “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction,” he said in his victory speech. Polls and pundits agree that AI played a significant role in the election. “Six months ago, if you had told me that 56% of voters would have left their polling places stating that concerns about AI were crucial or important to their vote, I would have looked at you like you had 10 heads,” said Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of the Tech Oversight Project, a Washington, D.C.-based watchdog and advocacy group. Yet some AI experts predict that the variety of Democrats’ AI priorities could lead to fractured policy approaches and watered-down legislation, while other party leaders on AI predicted a more cooperative result. “I think the Democrats are going to have a hard time wrangling their own perspectives on this,” said Samuel Hammond, director of AI policy at the Foundation for American Innovation, a right-leaning Washington, D.C., think tank. He highlighted the distance between proposals like the one championed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., to ban artificial superintelligence — referring to systems smarter than humans at all cognitive tasks — and more prosaic efforts to update permitting guidelines to build power plants and other AI-related infrastructure. Alex Bores, a New York Assembly member who authored one of the country’s most substantial pieces of AI legislation — the RAISE Act — disagreed. He framed candidates’ differing priorities as an asset that will allow Congress to tackle many critical AI policy initiatives simultaneously. Multiple policy approaches are “good and healthy as long as we’re working together to ensure that we are protecting the American people from the many different ways that this technology could harm people,” he said. “There is so much that we have to do in AI, foundational to who gets to decide what we’re building.” Bores also said that pro-AI funding had proved toxic to some candidates, pointing to significant losses for candidates supported by pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future. The organization also spent heavily against Bores in his own primary campaign for Congress earlier this year, which he narrowly lost. AI experts also predicted that Washington’s previous AI proposals would likely be significantly reimagined under the new political order. Before the election, a bipartisan bill co-sponsored by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., called the FRONTIER Act had worked its way through Washington as one of the most likely pieces of legislation to pass. The bill would require increased independent testing and oversight of the most advanced AI systems and mandate that leading AI companies create and publish safety-focused plans. However, Obernolte has faced an unusually competitive re-election battle. As of Sunday morning, his race had not been decided, according to NBC News. Congress has not passed a significant AI law in recent years, in large part because Trump has opposed regulation. The president and his allies, many of whom hail from Silicon Valley’s tech circles, have insisted that legislation will stifle America’s economy and the AI industry. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post in late August. The Trump administration has repeatedly endorsed federal bills that would pre-empt, or override, state-level legislation. David Sacks, the former White House AI czar and current chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, has said that state laws would lead to a harmful “patchwork” of legislation. Yet Tuesday’s results point to increasing bipartisan interest in passing meaningful AI legislation, according to the Foundation for American Innovation’s Hammond. “AI is not nearly as left-right polarized as most other issues,” he said. “Post-midterms, I think Republicans will feel less pressure from tech money and have, at least in the short run, greater degrees of freedom to express their parallel concerns about AI,” he added.

articles.title: Jewellery craftsman vanishes with 276g of gold worth ₹27.6L
articles.summary: Ahmedabad jewellery artisan alleges worker fled with 276.05g gold ornaments worth ₹27.6 lakh entrusted for setting work; FIR filed after calls went unanswered.
articles.body: Ahmedabad: A 50-year-old gold jewellery artisan from Ghatlodia has lodged a complaint alleging that a worker he entrusted with gold ornaments for setting work disappeared with jewellery weighing 276.05g and valued at Rs 27.6 lakh.The complainant told police that he works from home and has been in the jewellery-making trade for several years. He collected ornaments from traders on CG Road and had intricate setting work done by different workers before returning the finished pieces to the traders.On Oct 28, he collected a gold necklace set weighing 184.9g and a pair of earrings weighing 49.5g from a jeweller near Girish Coldrinks. Two days later, he handed these to the accused, a resident of Nirnay Nagar, for setting work. On Oct 31, the complainant collected four gold pieces weighing 21.8g and another pair of earrings weighing 35.2g from the same jeweller and gave the four pieces to the accused on Nov 2, retaining the earrings. On Nov 1, too, the accused had allegedly been handed 19.9g of gold for setting stones in jewellery.When he called Soni on Nov 2 to collect the earlier consignment, the artisan did not answer his calls. articles.title: Israeli forces release Palestinian journalist Abou Shhadeh
articles.summary: Abed Abou Shhadeh says his detention was part of Israel’s political measures ‘to intimidate Arab society as a whole’.
articles.body:
Israeli authorities have released Palestinian journalist Abed Abou Shhadeh after detaining him for five days without charge.

Speaking after his release, Abou Shhadeh said on Sunday that his detention was part of “political measures” intended not only for him “but to intimidate Arab society as a whole”.

“In my view, the most appropriate response is to reaffirm among ourselves that we are on the right side, that our path is the path of truth,” he said, adding that he would continue his work as a journalist.

Abou Shhadeh was held in a Shin Bet intelligence facility in Petah Tikva, on the outskirts of Tel Aviv, after being detained on Tuesday on suspicion of “contact with a foreign agent”.

He was suspected of receiving money from foreign sources in order to support Israel’s Arab voters, according to the legal rights group Adalah, which is part of his defence team.

The accusation came after Abou Shhadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, spoke on the al-Midan podcast for the Arab48 website and appeared as an analyst on Al Jazeera.

He addressed topics similar to those discussed in Israeli media outlets, according to Hadeel Abu Salih, his legal counsel and a human rights lawyer with Adalah.

“It was obvious from the first day, from Thursday, that the police doesn’t have, any evidence in this context,” Abu Salih said. All of the suspicion relied on a public conversation he had with Palestinian intellectual Azmi Bishara when he was in Qatar.

“This is now being criminalised only because the speakers are Palestinians,” Abu Salih said. “Or when Palestinians are asking to analyse their political reality. The Israeli system turned that discussion and analysis into a criminal suspicion.”

“They were trying to say that he’s not a journalist, that he’s a political counsel.”

The lawyer said Abou Shhadeh was arrested in the middle of the night on Tuesday after 15 Israeli security officers raided his home in Jaffa and confiscated personal belongings, such as electronic devices and books, in front of his two children.

‘Campaign against the votes of… Palestinians’

His five-day detention was “part of the campaign against the votes of the Arabs and Palestinians in Israel”, Adalah founder Hassan Jabareen told Al Jazeera.

Jabareen said Israel sought to “delegitimise their votes” by the claims against Abou Shhadeh.

“He travelled to Doha as a journalist … he came back as a journalist. But he was arrested as an Arab political person,” Jabareen said. “They tried to use him in order to say that Arabs use illegal [means] in their political participation in the Israeli elections. ”

articles.title: Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant loses power again, relying on generators for electricity
articles.summary: The Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine has lost its external electricity supply again, forcing it to rely on
articles.body: The Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine has lost its external electricity supply again, forcing it to rely on emergency diesel generators to keep its reactors cool and maintain essential safety functions, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Sunday.The plant's connection to its only remaining external power line, Ferosplavna-1, was lost early on Sunday. This marks the 27th such incident since the Russia-Ukraine conflict began in February 2022, highlighting continuing concerns over nuclear safety at the site."The cause and location of the latest disconnection are not yet known," the IAEA said in a post on X. It added that the plant had enough fuel to operate a limited number of emergency diesel generators for around two weeks.IAEA director general Rafael Grossi stressed the need to restore the plant's connection to the power grid and increase its diesel fuel reserves.The plant's Russian-installed management said the power line had been disconnected by "automatic protection". It added that radiation levels at the facility and in the surrounding surveillance zone remained normal.The plant, Europe's largest nuclear facility with six reactors, was seized by Russian forces in the early weeks of the invasion. It no longer generates electricity but requires an external power supply to keep nuclear fuel cool.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Train crash kills seven, injures dozens near Egypt’s Cairo city
articles.summary: The passenger train was travelling from Egypt’s capital to Aswan in the south when it derailed, overturning carriages.
articles.body:
At least seven people have been killed and more than 112 others injured in a train crash on the outskirts of Cairo in Egypt’s Giza province, according to the country’s Health Ministry.

A train travelling between Giza and Fayoum on Sunday ran into the back of another train on the Cairo-to-Aswan route, causing the latter to derail from its tracks onto a countryside road in the district of al-Ayyat, authorities said.

Emergency rescue teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, Egyptian National Railways said.

Authorities say more than 70 ambulances were involved in transport and evacuation operations at the scene of the crash, with casualties taken to nearby hospitals.

Al-Ayyat district, where the collision happened, is also the site of Egypt’s worst-ever rail disaster .

In 2002, more than 370 people were killed when a fire swept through a train carrying holiday travellers south of Cairo. In 2009, multiple train crashes in the area killed dozens.

Egypt’s 110 million people depend heavily on rail transport, but the cross-country network – one of the largest in Africa – is in need of modernisation.

Over the past decade, Egypt has poured billions of dollars into updating its transport infrastructure, including new highways and high-speed rail lines, but has yet to overhaul much of its dated train services .

articles.title: In 2015, a Louisiana woman began a long legal fight over neighbours using a rural road beside her home; in November 2026, appeals judges upheld her right to stop them using the private section beyond its first 1,000 feet
articles.summary: Living beside a quiet country road in French Settlement, Louisiana, Mona Matherne spent more than ten years trying to stop her neighbours from using a
articles.body: Living beside a quiet country road in French Settlement, Louisiana, Mona Matherne spent more than ten years trying to stop her neighbours from using a private stretch of land that passes her home. On Friday, 6 November 2026, state appeals judges brought the long-running dispute to an end. They ruled that the 73-year-old landowner has the legal right to stop her neighbours from driving beyond the first 1,000 feet of the unpaved road. The Louisiana Court of Appeal for the First Circuit upheld an earlier decision in the case of Mona Matherne v. Marshall and Mark Parker. The dispute first went to the local courts in 2015. The appeals court also confirmed her property rights and kept a permanent court order in place. The order prevents her neighbours from entering the private section of the road or harassing her in any way.Origin of the decade long rural boundary feudMatherne bought her country home at 18400 Legion Road in French Settlement in 2007. Her property runs along the eastern side of the road, which connects directly to Louisiana Highway 16. Her neighbours, Mark Parker and his relative Marshall Parker, own land further along the road. Mark owns land directly across from Matherne, while Marshall owns a nearby property. The disagreement started when Matherne noticed that the Parkers regularly used the full length of Legion Road to reach their properties. This meant driving past her home and crossing land that she said belonged entirely to her. In 2015, Matherne asked a court in Livingston Parish to stop them from using the road. She argued that Legion Road was not public beyond its first section and accused the Parkers of trespassing on her land. She also reported several incidents of threatening behaviour. She claimed that Mark Parker had repeatedly confronted and threatened her. She further accused him of displaying a firearm during separate incidents. The Parkers denied the accusations and said they had a legal right to use the road. They argued that Legion Road had become public through a legal process known as "tacit dedication". They said parish officials had maintained the road several times over the years, which they believed had made the entire stretch a public road.Court findings on public road dedicationThe case went through several years of court hearings and reviews of evidence. In 2016, the court first issued a temporary order in Matherne's favour, limiting how the Parkers could use the road. After reviewing detailed evidence about past road maintenance and property records, the 21st Judicial District Court delivered its final decision on 30 December 2024. The court ruled that the first 1,000 feet of Legion Road, starting from Highway 16, was a public road. However, the rest of the road was private property owned by Matherne. "The trial court found that the portion of Legion Road past the first 1,000 feet is private property and not a public roadway," the court record stated. The trial judge also issued a permanent order stopping Mark and Marshall Parker from driving beyond the 1,000-foot point. They were also told to stop contacting or harassing Matherne. The Parkers later challenged the decision under docket number 2026 CA 0464. They argued that the trial judge had wrongly applied Louisiana property laws about public roads and had made a mistake by issuing the permanent order.Appellate ruling confirms private property protectionsAccording to a report published by Laws.com, the First Circuit Court of Appeal rejected the Parkers' arguments and upheld the lower court's decision in full. The appeals judges found that the Parkers had not provided enough evidence to show that parish workers had maintained the upper section of Legion Road regularly or extensively enough to make it a public road under Louisiana law. The court explained that occasional repairs or maintenance by local public workers do not automatically take away a landowner's private property rights. There must be clear evidence that the public intended to use the road and that it received regular maintenance over a long period before a private road can be treated as public. The ruling keeps the permanent court order in place. This protects Matherne's right to put up private property signs and stop vehicles from travelling beyond the 1,000-foot point. Court records also confirm that the Parkers could face legal penalties for contempt of court if they drive beyond the public section of the road or try to contact Matherne.You use AI every day.
